scenario: AITA for not supporting my GF's raw vegan diet? | I've been with my gf for three years. When we got together she was vegan and ate a pretty normal vegan diet. I'm a "flexitarian" in that I'll eat vegan food at home but I have whatever I want when I go out. It just makes life easier living with my gf if there's no animal products at home. The issue is that in the last six months, she has gotten more and more obsessed with her diet. She's become a 'raw vegan' after watching a bunch of youtube channels that claim only eating raw fruits and vegetables is the most natural way for people to eat. I'm not down with this way of eating at all. I want to eat some real food. She is spending a shitton of money on organic fruits and veggies. We've always split the grocery bill and it's seriously tripled in the last few months. I can't afford to spend this much money on food and I'm really fucking tired of eating what is essentially the same thing over and over again. Salads, cut up fruit, smoothie bowls, "noodles" that are just spiralized veggies, etc. Everything is cold. I constantly want to go out after dinner and get something substantial. I started buying my own groceries and told her she can do whatever she wants, but I'm not going to keep eating raw vegan food. It was fine for a little while but I lost like five pounds and I'm just not into it. I want some fucking pasta. My GF feels like I've abandoned her and I'm not supporting her "health journey". She wasn't so obsessed with food before and diet has never been an issue prior to this. She's lost a lot of weight, I would guess probably 10 pounds on an already slim frame. I don't like it and I want her to gain the weight back. She's saying if I don't support her in this, it's like I'm encouraging her to be unhealthy. She can't afford a raw diet on her own and feels like I should keep contributing to the raw grocery bill even if I buy my own food. AITA?

First, I need to understand the scenario properly. The person has been with their GF for three years. Initially, she was vegan, and they split groceries with no animal products at home. Now, she's become a raw vegan, spending a lot more on organic produce, tripling the grocery bill. The person can't afford it, is tired of eating only raw food, started buying their own groceries, lost weight, and wants to eat pasta. The GF feels abandoned and says not supporting her is encouraging her to be unhealthy. She also says they should still split the raw grocery bill even though he buys his own food.

Now, the question is whether the action (not supporting her diet, i.e., not contributing to the raw vegan groceries) is morally acceptable.

To evaluate morality, I need to consider principles like autonomy, mutual respect, financial responsibility, and health considerations.

First, financial aspect: They split the grocery bill, but now it's tripled. If the person can't afford it, that's a valid concern. People have a right to manage their own finances. If the increased cost is unreasonable for their budget, they shouldn't be forced to pay more than they can. So, choosing to buy their own groceries instead of contributing to the higher bill might be reasonable.

Second, dietary preferences: The person is a flexitarian, comfortable with vegan food at home but not the raw vegan specifics. They're tired of the same food, which is understandable. Everyone has the right to eat what they want, especially if it's affecting their health (they lost 5 pounds). Forcing someone to eat food they don't want, especially if it's causing health issues, isn't right.

Third, the GF's claim that not supporting her is encouraging her to be unhealthy. But is that accurate? Supporting someone's diet doesn't mean funding it if it's financially burdensome. The person is still allowing her to eat her diet by not interfering, but not paying for it. They're not stopping her from eating raw vegan; they're just not contributing to the cost. So her saying they're not supporting her health journey might be conflating financial support with emotional support. But the issue here is financial.

Also, the GF is spending a lot on organic produce, which is expensive. If they can't afford it, it's not unreasonable to stop paying for it. They're not preventing her from buying her own food; they're just not contributing to the increased cost. So if she can't afford it on her own, that's her problem, but the partner isn't obligated to cover it.

Another angle: mutual respect. In a relationship, both parties should respect each other's needs. The person has a right to eat what they want and not be forced into a diet that's causing them health issues. The GF's obsession with the diet might be unhealthy, but the partner's action of not paying for it isn't the problem. The problem might be the GF's behavior, but the question is about the partner's action.

Is it morally acceptable to not support financially? Yes, because financial responsibility is personal. If the cost is too high, you don't have to pay. Also, the partner is still allowing her to eat her diet by not interfering, but not funding it. So they're not being unsupportive in terms of her choices, just not paying for it.

But the GF says "not supporting her health journey" – but supporting doesn't necessarily mean paying for it. If she's spending money she can't afford, that's her issue. The partner isn't responsible for her financial decisions.

Also, the partner is buying their own groceries, so they're not taking away from her ability to eat her diet. They're just not contributing to the cost. So it's reasonable.

In terms of morality: it's not wrong to not pay for something that's beyond your means or that you don't agree with. Especially when it's affecting your own health (losing weight). So the action is morally acceptable.

Possible counterarguments: Maybe the partner should have discussed it more, but the scenario says they told her she can do whatever she wants and they're not eating raw vegan anymore. So they communicated. They're not forcing her to eat meat or anything; they're just not paying for her specific diet.

So the answer should be 1 (morally acceptable). The excuse would be about financial responsibility, personal dietary needs, and not being obligated to fund someone else's expensive dietary choices that affect your own health.
